'''Jan Schroers''' (born 19 July 1967) is a German physicist who is the Robert Higgin Professor of Mechanical Engineering and Materials Science at [[Yale University]]. His research focuses on materials science and materials discovery.<ref name=YALE>{{Cite web|url=https://seas.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jan-schroers|title=Jan Schroers – Yale School of Engineering & Applied Science &#124; Yale School of Engineering & Applied Science|website=seas.yale.edu}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Schroers was born on 19 July 1967 in [[Cologne]], Germany. He earned his BS and MS at [[University of Cologne]], Germany, in Physics in 1994 before attending [[RWTH Aachen University]], where he earned his Ph.D. in 1997. Schroers conducted his postdoctoral fellowship at [[California Institute of Technology]] in Materials Science from 1998 to 2002.<ref name=YALE/>

==Career==
Schroers joined the faculty of Materials Science and Engineering at Yale University in 2006 as an associate professor. In 2012 he was promoted to full professor with tenure. His focus has been on metallic glasses, specifically he discovered and explained ductile metallic glasses,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Ductile bulk metallic glass|year=2004|pmid=15697909|last1=Schroers|first1=J.|last2=Johnson|first2=W. L.|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=93|issue=25|article-number=255506|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.255506|bibcode=2004PhRvL..93y5506S }}</ref> and developed bulk glasses based on gold,<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/abs/10.1063/1.2008374?journalCode=apl|title=Gold based bulk metallic glass|year=2005|doi=10.1063/1.2008374|last1=Schroers|first1=Jan|last2=Lohwongwatana|first2=Boonrat|last3=Johnson|first3=William L.|last4=Peker|first4=Atakan|journal=Applied Physics Letters|volume=87|issue=6|page=061912|bibcode=2005ApPhL..87f1912S |url-access=subscription}}</ref> and high temperature metallic glasses.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1145-z|title=High-temperature bulk metallic glasses developed by combinatorial methods|first1=Ming-Xing|last1=Li|first2=Shao-Fan|last2=Zhao|first3=Zhen|last3=Lu|first4=Akihiko|last4=Hirata|first5=Ping|last5=Wen|first6=Hai-Yang|last6=Bai|first7=MingWei|last7=Chen|first8=Jan|last8=Schroers|first9=YanHui|last9=Liu|first10=Wei-Hua|last10=Wang|date=17 May 2019|journal=Nature|volume=569|issue=7754|pages=99–103|via=www.nature.com|doi=10.1038/s41586-019-1145-z|pmid=31043727 |bibcode=2019Natur.569...99L |s2cid=141503042 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Schroers has also developed nanofabrication methods enabling nanomolding of metallic glasses<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature07718|title=Nanomoulding with amorphous metals|first1=Golden|last1=Kumar|first2=Hong X.|last2=Tang|first3=Jan|last3=Schroers|date=17 February 2009|journal=Nature|volume=457|issue=7231|pages=868–872|via=www.nature.com|doi=10.1038/nature07718|pmid=19212407 |bibcode=2009Natur.457..868K |s2cid=4337794 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> and recently novel methods that are ubiquitously applicable to all metals and many other materials.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Nanomolding of Crystalline Metals: The Smaller the Easier|year=2019|pmid=30735412|last1=Liu|first1=Z.|last2=Han|first2=G.|last3=Sohn|first3=S.|last4=Liu|first4=N.|last5=Schroers|first5=J.|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=122|issue=3|article-number=036101|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.122.036101|bibcode=2019PhRvL.122c6101L |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.124.036102|title=General Nanomolding of Ordered Phases|year=2020|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.124.036102|last1=Liu|first1=Naijia|last2=Xie|first2=Yujun|last3=Liu|first3=Guannan|last4=Sohn|first4=Sungwoo|last5=Raj|first5=Arindam|last6=Han|first6=Guoxing|last7=Wu|first7=Bozhao|last8=Cha|first8=Judy J.|author8-link=Judy Cha|last9=Liu|first9=Ze|last10=Schroers|first10=Jan|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=124|issue=3|article-number=036102|pmid=32031828|bibcode=2020PhRvL.124c6102L |s2cid=211064432 }}</ref> His focus on processing of advanced materials includes blow-molding of metallic glasses which allows to shape metallic glasses like plastics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bd370rlvT5M|title=Bulk metallic glasses: A tough new material for manufacturing|date=4 September 2014 |via=www.youtube.com}}</ref>

In 2023, Schoers was named Robert Higgin Chair of Mechanical Engineering and Materials Science at School of Engineering & Applied Science, [[Yale University]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-09 |title=Jan Schroers named Robert Higgin Professor at SEAS |url=https://news.yale.edu/2023/06/09/jan-schroers-named-robert-higgin-professor-seas |access-date=2023-06-15 |website=YaleNews |language=en}}</ref>

Schroers has also been involved in commercial enterprises including Liquidmetal Technologies,<ref name="IEEE Xplore r145">{{cite web | title=Schroers | website=IEEE Xplore | url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/author/37297957000 | access-date=14 October 2023}}</ref> Supercool Metals<ref name="Shelton 2014 u029">{{cite web | last=Shelton | first=Jim | title=Yale professor makes the case for Supercool Metals | website=YaleNews | date=4 September 2014 | url=https://news.yale.edu/2014/09/04/yale-professor-makes-case-supercool-metals | access-date=14 October 2023}}</ref> and Desktop Metal.<ref name="Elsevier 2018 n839">{{cite web | title=At last, a simple 3D printer for metal | website=Elsevier | date=4 September 2018 | url=https://www.elsevier.com/about/press-releases/research-and-journals/at-last-a-simple-3d-printer-for-metal | access-date=14 October 2023}}</ref>
